God. Philosophically, understood as the transcendent, supreme being in Western religious and philosophical traditions—variously conceived as infinite, omnipotent, omniscient, and morally perfect. Philosophers have constructed elaborate arguments for God's existence and debated God's nature intensely. God is both a core religious concept and a central topic in metaphysics, epistemology, and philosophy of religion. The question of God's existence has shaped Western philosophy from ancient times through the present, driving major developments in logic, metaphysics, and natural theology.

Descartes offered a proof of God through the idea of the infinite. He argued that only an infinite being could implant the idea of infinity in a finite mind like ours. Thomas Aquinas developed the Five Ways—five arguments for God's existence derived from motion, causality, contingency, degrees of perfection, and the cosmic order itself. The ontological argument, formulated by Anselm, claims that God necessarily exists because God is defined as the greatest conceivable being, and existence is greater than non-existence.

There is, however, the problem of evil. If God is omnipotent and good, why does evil exist? Philosophers have developed theodicies—complex arguments attempting to reconcile God's perfection with the flawed world we experience. Medieval theology, especially in Aquinas, also grappled with how to reconcile God's omniscience with human free will. If God knows all future choices with certainty, are those choices truly free? This remains a deep philosophical puzzle.

Modern philosophy has increasingly questioned whether God-existence claims are rationally justifiable. Atheism and agnosticism have emerged as serious philosophical positions. The question is whether faith in God transcends rational proof or whether belief requires rational justification. This remains one of philosophy's most profound and divisive questions.
